worst_places.before: `next/font` downloads the font **at build time**, self-hosts the file as a static asset, and automatically generates `@font-face` with `size-adjust` — meaning: no runtime request to Google Fonts (which itself improves privacy — the user's IP isn't sent to Google on every page load), and the fallback font's metrics are tuned to occupy a size as close as possible to the real font, minimizing CLS on swap.
worst_places.after: `next/font` does three things. First, it downloads the font **at build time** and serves it from your own domain as a static asset. So there is no runtime request to Google Fonts. That also improves privacy: the user's IP address is never sent to Google on a page load. Second, it generates `@font-face` with `size-adjust`, which tunes the fallback font's metrics to take up almost the same space as the real font. That way the text barely moves when the real font swaps in, so CLS stays low.

worst_places.before:
## Context

Before Next.js 13, the only option was the **Pages Router** — a `pages/` file structure where every file is a page, and a page is a React component that's server-rendered on the initial request and then hydrated as a regular Client Component. Next.js 13 introduced the **App Router** (`app/` directory), built around React Server Components (RSC), nested layouts, and streaming.
worst_places.after:
## The short version

Next.js has two routers, and you need both in practice: the **App Router** for new code, the **Pages Router** because it is what most existing codebases still use. The difference that matters is the default component model — in the App Router a page is a Server Component; in the Pages Router it is a Client Component.

The **Pages Router** was the only option before Next.js 13. Its rule: a `pages/` file structure where every file is a page, and a page is a React component. That component is server-rendered on the initial request, then hydrated as a regular Client Component. Next.js 13 introduced the **App Router** (the `app/` directory), built around React Server Components (RSC), nested layouts, and streaming.

patterns: MOST IMPORTANT — abbreviations are expanded in the article that OWNS them and nowhere else. Article 02 correctly expands CSR/SSR/SSG/ISR in its H2 headings; article 07 correctly expands CLS, FOUT, FOIT; article 09 correctly defines the big four in its numbered answers. But article 01 — the entry point that a new reader opens FIRST — uses SSR 9×, SSG 6×, SPA 5×, plus CSR/ISR/RSC/SEO/TTFB/FCP/TTI/CLS/DOM/CRA/FOIT/FOUT/SWR and expands not one of them. Same shape in 04 (RSC in the very first code block, never expanded), 07 (LCP used 6× in prose, expanded 45 lines later in a table), 09 (CLS/LCP/INP used in Q54-55, defined in Q56). The habit is 'it's explained in the article about it', which the rubric explicitly rejects — and the fix is mechanical: move the existing expansion to the first mention in each file.

The EN files are systematically harder than the RU files, and the cause is structural, not lexical: the RU sentence pattern 'claim — mechanism (parenthetical caveat) — consequence' joined by em-dashes survives translation intact, and English's extra articles and prepositions push it over the limit. Long-sentence rates: ru/06 6.1% vs en/06 31.9%; ru/07 26.8% vs en/07 40.5%; ru/04 15.4% vs en/04 30.8%. Worst single sentences are 66w (en/07 next-font), 56w (en/09 loading/error), 52w (en/06 template). Fix: at translation time, break every em-dash chain into separate sentences instead of preserving it.

Every RU file has an English or code-switched H1: 5 are fully English (`# Next.js Fundamentals`, `# Rendering Models: CSR, SSR, SSG, ISR`, `# App Router vs Pages Router`, `# Server Components vs Client Components`, `# Next.js Interview Questions (Middle → Senior)`) and the other 4 are hybrids glued with «и» (`# Data Fetching, Caching и Revalidation`, `# Routing, Layouts и Middleware`, `# SEO, Metadata и Performance`, `# Production Architecture и Best Practices`). The pattern extends into H2s: `## Practical пример: e-commerce страница товара` (ru/05), `## Client Component — explicit opt-in` (ru/04), `## Четыре уровня кеширования в Next.js — must-know для senior` (ru/05).

Three RU files contain raw untranslated English words wedged into Russian grammar — «— это means:» (ru/07), «Нюанс specific для App Router» (ru/08), «было source of truth для» where the EN says 'root cause' (ru/05) — plus one Latin letter inside a Cyrillic word, «крауlер» (ru/09), and a missing space after a comma («сборки**,self-host'ит», ru/07). These are not stylistic anglicisms, they are un-proofread machine-translation residue. They cluster in files 05, 07, 08, 09 — i.e. the later half of the topic, which suggests the pass ran out of attention.

Sections tend to open with interview meta-framing rather than the fact: `## Уровень вопросов` / `## The level of these questions` (08, a paragraph about who asks these questions before any architecture), `## Четыре уровня кеширования — must-know для senior` opening with «Один из самых частых senior-вопросов…» (05), `## Контекст` / `## Context` opening with history about the Pages Router in an article about the App Router (03). The rest of the zone gets this right — ru/04 opens with `## SSR ≠ Server Components — главное, что нужно развести в голове` and answers immediately, which is the model the other files should follow.
notes: Strengths worth protecting: D (4.0) and E (3.8) are genuinely good — nearly every new concept lands on a code block or a `txt` diagram within a line or two, examples are short, self-contained and commented at the non-obvious line, and the model-comparison tables in 02/03/07/08 are excellent for phone reading. Do not touch those. Verdict is `targeted-fixes` rather than `systemic-refactor` because no restructuring is needed: the required edits are (1) an abbreviation-first-use pass per file, (2) an EN sentence-splitting pass, (3) nine H1 translations, (4) five named RU translation artifacts. That said, criterion B on the EN half (avg 2.4) is borderline systemic — all nine EN files need the sentence pass, not a handful of places. Two technical inconsistencies noticed in passing, outside the readability scope: ru+en/05 call `cookies()` synchronously while ru+en/02 teach that it became async in Next.js 15; ru+en/04 use `useState` in `ClientWrapper` without importing it, though the `Counter` example two blocks earlier does import it.
